title: Freud and Lacan
keyWorks: S. Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams (1900)
S. Freud, Civilization and Its Discontents (1930)
J. Lacan, “The Mirror Stage as Formative of the Function of the I” (1949)
J. Lacan, Seminar VII: The Ethics of Psychoanalysis (1959–1960)
J. Lacan, Seminar XI: The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis (1964)
summary: Psychoanalysis, created by Sigmund Freud and rethought by Jacques Lacan, starts from the idea that much of our mental life is unconscious — that is, it operates without our knowing. Lacan added that the unconscious is “structured like a language,” and that the human being is a desiring creature whose desire is born of lack.
onEmotions: For psychoanalysis, feelings are not malfunctions but messages: through them speaks what we don’t yet know about ourselves. Freud showed that an affect can “move” from one thought to another, so the cause of a feeling is not always where it seems to be. Lacan insisted that desire is always bound up with the Other — with language, culture, the people whose recognition we seek. The task is not to get rid of a feeling but to find words for it. Here we explain ideas rather than give clinical advice: psychoanalysis is, above all, a conversation.

anxiety.text: Lacan asks you to picture yourself before a giant female praying mantis, wearing a mask you can’t see — so you don’t know what she takes you for. That is anxiety for him, an agonizing feeling with nothing shameful in it. Freud saw it first as a “dammed-up” drive, then as a signal of something the psyche can’t yet cope with. Lacan went further: anxiety, he argues, is “not without an object”: it arises when we come too close to the desire of the Other — to the question “What do they want from me?” — and don’t know the answer. So Lacan considered anxiety the most trustworthy affect: it points to something genuine, even if we can’t name it. So anxiety doesn’t have to be silenced straight away: you can listen to it as a messenger who has come on real business.
anxiety.practice: Ask yourself aloud, as Lacan did: “Che vuoi? What do you want from me?” — and picture who the question is addressed to. No need to answer: it’s enough to notice whose face appears.

quote.text: Anxiety is that which does not deceive.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan

fear.text: Five-year-old Hans was afraid to go outside: horses might fall down and bite. His case, taken up by Freud and later Lacan, explains much about fear, which often protects you. Freud distinguished fear from anxiety: fear has a definite object — a dog, an exam, a difficult conversation — while anxiety is diffuse and nameless. Curiously, psychoanalysis sometimes sees fear as a kind of relief. In Hans’s case Freud showed that this fear gathered a vaguer anxiety around a single image and gave it shape. Lacan later said that such an object of fear serves as a support: it sets a boundary where otherwise there would be formless anxiety. So your fear probably has a direct meaning, but it may carry something else as well. Acknowledging fear doesn’t oblige you to conquer it at once — it’s enough to ask what it is saying besides the obvious.
fear.practice: Draw your fear the way Hans might have drawn a horse — one quick outline, no beauty. Then ask the drawing: “Apart from you, what am I afraid of?” — and notice what comes to mind.

sadness.text: In 1973 Lacan appeared on French television and called sadness “moral cowardice.” If you are sad right now, that sounds hurtful — but sadness needs no justification, and Lacan wasn’t talking about weakness at all. Freud saw sorrow as the normal work of a psyche learning to let go of something dear. Lacan meant not a reproach to the person but a retreat from the duty of “speaking well” (bien dire) — finding the precise words for one’s desire. Sadness, for Lacan, often appears where desire has fallen silent, where we have stopped asking what we really want. This sounds stern, but there is hope in it too: sadness is not a verdict but a sign that some desire is waiting to be named. You don’t have to drive sadness away; you can let it lead you to that unspoken word.
sadness.practice: Say aloud one sentence beginning with “What I would really like is…”, and don’t correct it. Lacan would call this an attempt at “speaking well” — bien dire.

grief.text: When Freud’s father died, he wrote to a friend that he felt “torn up by the roots” — and out of that loss grew The Interpretation of Dreams. Grief is a natural response to loss, not an illness. In “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), Freud described the “work of mourning”: the psyche returns again and again to every memory, every hope connected with what was lost, and gradually, piece by piece, lets them go. It is slow and painful, and there’s no need to rush it. Lacan added that loss tears “a hole in the real” — in the very fabric of life — and a person fills it with symbols: words, rituals, farewells. That is why funerals, anniversaries, stories about someone who is no longer here matter so much: they help express loss when it seems there are no words. Grief is the labor of love, not its end.
grief.practice: Tell someone — or yourself, aloud — one concrete detail about what you have lost: a gesture, a smell, a phrase. Lacan would say that this is how the hole in the real slowly gathers words around it.

loneliness.text: “There is no sexual relationship” — this line of Lacan’s is often taken as cynical, though for someone who feels very lonely right now it can bring a strange comfort. Freud wrote that a human being begins life in a state of complete helplessness (Hilflosigkeit) and so needs another from the very start. Lacan added a sober thought to this — that very formula. He meant that two people never add up to a whole without remainder: their desires never fully coincide. You can hear this as sad news, or as freeing news: your loneliness doesn’t prove that something is wrong with you. Everyone has a certain separateness, even in the closest relationships. And it is precisely thanks to this gap between people that speech, desire and encounter are possible.
loneliness.practice: Stand at a window for a minute and look at the lit windows opposite or at passers-by: each of them has their own separateness too. Say to yourself: “The gap is not emptiness but a place for speech.”

anger.text: Lacan liked a line he attributed to Charles Péguy: anger is when the little pegs won’t go into the little holes. A funny image for a living, legitimate feeling, but an accurate one: anger says that something matters to you and something didn’t fit. In “Aggressivity in Psychoanalysis” (1948), Lacan linked aggression to the “mirror stage”: we build our ego by recognizing ourselves in an image — in a mirror or in another person. So the other both resembles us and seems to occupy our place, and this gives rise to rivalry. Anger often flares up precisely in this “imaginary,” mirror-like field: “they’re just like me, but they pulled it off.” The pegs and holes are also about reality not fitting the expected order. Seen this way, anger doesn’t make you a bad person; it shows where something didn’t match.
anger.practice: Go to a mirror and look at your face while you are angry — just look, as if at someone else’s. Ask: “Who am I competing with right now — the person, or their image?”

shame.text: A man peeps through a keyhole — and suddenly hears footsteps behind him. Lacan loved retelling this scene from Sartre, because all of shame, painful and deeply human, is in it. For Lacan, shame is closely tied to the gaze. In The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis he describes the gaze as one of the forms of the “object a” — his name for what causes our desire and anxiety yet can never be fully grasped. Shame is the moment when you suddenly find yourself seen, as if caught in the act, and cannot control how you are seen. Importantly, this gaze is often more imagined than real: we feel ashamed before an Other we carry inside ourselves. Understanding this doesn’t cancel shame, but it loosens its grip a little.
shame.practice: Look at any object in the room and recall Lacan’s story of the sardine can floating in the sea: “You see that can? Well, it doesn’t see you!” For a minute, be invisible to things: shame loves an imaginary onlooker, and things don’t look.

guilt.text: “The only thing one can be guilty of is having given ground relative to one’s desire” — so Lacan summed up his seminar on ethics. If guilt is weighing on you heavily right now, that doesn’t mean you are a bad person. In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), Freud described a strange paradox of the “superego” — the inner agency that watches and judges: the more a person submits to its demands and renounces their desires, the stricter it becomes. That is why guilt is often strongest in the most conscientious people. In The Ethics of Psychoanalysis, Lacan turned the question around: guilt is about betraying what really matters to you. This is not a call to do whatever you like, but a question of being true to yourself. It helps to distinguish real responsibility for a specific act from an endless inner tribunal that always demands more.
guilt.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “what I’m really responsible for” and “what the superego accuses me of.” Read the second column aloud in the voice of a strict judge — and notice how it sounds from outside.

envy.text: Augustine recalls an infant who cannot yet speak but already turns pale with envy, watching his foster brother at the breast. People tend to hide envy, but everyone knows it — even someone who has no words yet. Lacan loved this example from the Confessions and noted that the little one is already fed himself — he envies not the milk but the picture of another’s fullness, an image in which the other seems whole and satisfied. That is envy in general: we rarely want the thing itself; we want the happiness we imagine it gives the other. Hence Lacan’s famous idea that our desire is born through the Other. Once you see this, envy becomes a clue rather than a verdict: it shows what image of fullness attracts you — and reminds you that the person you envy has a lack of their own.
envy.practice: Imagine you got what you envy and lived with it for a week. What changed? If the picture fades quickly, you were envying not the thing but an image of someone else’s fullness.

quote.text: Man’s desire is the desire of the Other.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar XI: The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis (1964)

emptiness.text: A potter shapes a vase around emptiness: that is how Lacan explained where desire comes from. Feeling empty and wanting nothing is not laziness or whim. Freud noticed a difference: in mourning the world seems poor; in melancholia the ego itself feels poor and empty. He explained it this way: when a loss is not recognized, “the shadow of the object falls upon the ego,” and a person seems to lose a part of themselves. Lacan offered another view: emptiness is not always an enemy. Remember the potter: without the void there is no vessel. Lack, for Lacan, is the place from which desire is born. Perhaps your emptiness is not an absence of life but a space where a new desire has not yet found its name. If it lasts a long time, it’s worth talking about it with someone you trust.
emptiness.practice: Cup your hands and hold them like that for a minute, looking at the emptiness between them. Ask: “If one small desire could appear here, what would it be?” “I don’t know” is an answer too.

quote.text: In mourning it is the world which has become poor and empty; in melancholia it is the ego itself.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

confusion.text: Freud once forgot the name of the painter Signorelli, and Botticelli and Boltraffio kept coming to mind instead — out of that small muddle he made a discovery. When familiar landmarks stop working, confusion can be the same kind of doorway. Freud called the discovery of the unconscious the third blow to human self-love — after Copernicus and Darwin: it turned out that our conscious ego does not run the whole of our mental life. Lacan wrote the subject as a barred letter, $: we are divided, not fully transparent to ourselves, and part of what drives us speaks through slips of the tongue, dreams, recurring situations. Confusion is not a malfunction but an honest moment when you touch that division. It doesn’t need to be hastily closed with a ready-made answer. Psychoanalysis values exactly such moments: something you didn’t know about yourself may sound in them.
confusion.practice: For one minute, say aloud whatever comes to mind — without choosing or reconciling, as on the analyst’s couch. Then ask yourself: which word surprised me?

quote.text: The ego is not master in its own house.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: “A Difficulty in the Path of Psycho-Analysis” (1917)

fatigue.text: “Enjoy!” — for Lacan, this is the cruelest order an inner voice can give us. The exhaustion you feel is real, and that order has a lot to do with it. Freud described the “superego” as an inner overseer whose demands can never be fully met. Lacan added an unexpected twist: the superego demands not only “you mustn’t” but also “enjoy!” — be happy, productive, successful. He called the superego an imperative of jouissance — a word that means not simple pleasure but a strained “too much” that verges on pain. Lacan also distinguished demand — which can be satisfied — from desire, which is never sated. Burnout can be understood as an attempt to answer the Other’s endless demand completely, as if it could be closed. Admitting that this is impossible is not defeat but relief.
fatigue.practice: Answer aloud the inner voice that keeps saying “just a bit more, you have to get it done”: “I hear you. Not today.” Say it calmly, like an analyst who ends the session on time.

boredom.text: Neither Freud nor Lacan wrote about boredom as such, but Lacan would probably begin with a question: where has the spark gone? Boredom seems trivial, yet it can be very oppressive — and it is an honest feeling. Lacan believed that desire rests on lack and on the “object a” — the cause of desire, the elusive spark that makes anything attract us at all. Boredom is perhaps the state in which the objects around us are there but the spark is not: everything is available, yet nothing calls. This doesn’t mean desire has vanished — it simply hasn’t yet found where to go. Sometimes boredom is a useful pause: when the world stops offering ready-made answers, you get a chance to notice your own interest, not an imposed one.
boredom.practice: Remember the last time you were truly interested, and tell someone about it in two sentences. Listen: what drew you then — the thing itself, or some spark in it?

joy.text: “Look, here is the world that seems so dangerous — a game for children!” That, for Freud, is what the strict superego, suddenly friendly, tells us in humour. Joy needs no justification; psychoanalysis greets it attentively but without naivety. Freud described the “pleasure principle”: the psyche strives to reduce tension and reach equilibrium. Lacan distinguished from pleasure jouissance — “enjoyment,” an excessive, intense experience that can border on pain. Joy is closer to pleasure: it is gentle and doesn’t demand “more and more.” Joy doesn’t have to be complete or eternal to be real. You can let it be small and simply stay in it.
joy.practice: Tell someone one funny or happy little thing from today — just so that it gets said. Spoken aloud, joy becomes a little more yours.

love.text: “To give what you don’t have” — that is how Lacan defined love. It sounds strange, yet it describes tenderness remarkably well. Lacan spoke of love paradoxically: in it we give not things or virtues but our own lack — the admission that we are missing something and that the other matters to us. To love, for Lacan, is to open up, not to present yourself as flawless. Freud, for his part, noted that in love we often repeat early attachments and see in the beloved reflections of figures from the past. This doesn’t devalue the feeling — it simply shows that it is connected to your whole history. Psychoanalysis takes love seriously: the analytic conversation itself, for Freud, rests on “transference,” that is, on love. Your tenderness is not weakness but the courage to reveal your lack.
love.practice: Say to someone you love — or silently, picturing their face — one sentence beginning with “I miss…” or “It matters to me that you…”. That is the Lacanian gift: not a thing, but your own lack.

quote.text: Love is giving what you don’t have.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan

gratitude.text: Melanie Klein put two words that seem like opposites side by side in the title of a book: Envy and Gratitude. Gratitude is a warm feeling, and Klein explained why it matters so much. Klein, a psychoanalyst of the generation after Freud, showed in that book (1957) that these feelings are two poles: envy spoils the good we receive, while gratitude lets us accept it and keep it inside. Lacan has another thought: every demand is, at bottom, a demand for love, and a gift is precious not for the object itself but for what it means: “you matter to me.” That is why gratitude often responds not to the thing but to the sign of attention. Allowing yourself to be grateful means admitting that you need others, and there is nothing humiliating in that.
gratitude.practice: Thank someone today for a sign of attention rather than for a thing: “thank you for remembering,” “thank you for noticing.” Lacan would say you are answering a demand for love.

hope.text: “The voice of the intellect is a soft one, but it does not rest till it has gained a hearing,” wrote Freud, a man of cautious hope. Hope helps you keep living, and psychoanalysis treats it with respect, but soberly. In The Future of an Illusion (1927), Freud called an illusion a belief in which wish-fulfilment plays the leading part; it isn’t necessarily an error, but it’s useful to see what exactly we want. He himself believed in the slow but persistent power of reason and understanding. Lacan described desire as a movement that slides from one object to another and never comes to a final rest. Hope is desire turned toward the future. It doesn’t need to know how everything will end; it’s enough that desire is alive and keeps searching.
hope.practice: Finish: “I hope that…”, and on the line below: “And behind that lies a desire for…”. Read the second line quietly, like that soft voice of the intellect, and see what has emerged in it.

nostalgia.text: “The finding of an object is in fact a refinding of it,” Freud wrote in 1905. Nostalgia, sweet and sad at once, is living proof of that line, and there is nothing childish about it. In Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality he meant that every new attachment partly seeks something very early and long lost: we don’t so much find as recognize. Lacan developed this idea: the lost object, in a sense, was never in our hands in the fullness with which we remember it. Nostalgia longs not so much for the past as it was, but for the image of fullness that the past holds for us. This doesn’t devalue your memories — they are real. But you might notice that longing for “back then” says a lot about your desire “now.”
nostalgia.practice: Name aloud one memory you miss and ask: what feeling from it would I like to find in my life today? Lacan would say that longing for “back then” speaks of desire “now.”

quote.text: The finding of an object is in fact a refinding of it.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905)

craving.text: “That’s not it” — Lacan saw this phrase as the formula of desire itself: whatever we get, a gap remains. When a sharp “I want it right now” rolls in, there is nothing shameful in it. Lacan distinguished three things: need (hunger, thirst), demand (a request addressed to another) and desire — what remains beyond them and is never fully satisfied. A craving promises: “This is it, and then everything will be fine.” But having got the thing, we often feel the familiar Lacanian “that’s not it.” A cigarette, a drink or a phone often takes the place of something else — something hard to name. This doesn’t make you weak; this is how desire works for everyone. What helps is not so much prohibition as a question: what exactly am I hoping to get in this second — calm, closeness, oblivion?
craving.practice: When a craving comes, say aloud: “If I got it right now, I would feel…” — and finish the sentence. The last word is what you are really looking for; stay with it for a minute before doing anything.

addiction.text: “Palliative measures” — that is what Freud, without any judgment, called the things people use to ease a life that is too hard. Addiction is not a moral failure but a circle that is genuinely hard to get out of. In Civilization and Its Discontents he listed them: distractions, substitutes, intoxicating substances. He acknowledged that the last of these act quickly, but soberly noted the cost: they drain energy that could go into changing one’s life. In Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud described the “repetition compulsion” — the psyche’s tendency to return to what brings no pleasure. Lacan linked this to jouissance — something beyond simple pleasure that holds us even when it causes pain. Psychoanalysis suggests not shaming yourself but starting to speak: what has been named loses some of its power.
addiction.practice: Say one sentence aloud: “This helps me not to feel…” — and finish it. Then think about who you could really say it to: someone close, a professional, or a mutual-help group.

quote.text: Life, as we find it, is too hard for us; it brings us too many pains, disappointments and impossible tasks. In order to bear it we cannot dispense with palliative measures.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

hangover.text: Who is this judge who wakes you the morning after, before the alarm does? Your body aches, anxiety, shame and gaps in memory pile on top — and none of it makes you a bad person. In Group Psychology, Freud wrote about festivals: in them familiar prohibitions are lifted for a while, and a person feels free. But then the “superego” returns — the inner agency that judges, forbids and punishes. A “moral hangover” is the return of a strict inner judge who sometimes punishes far more harshly than what happened deserves. Lacan would add: the anxiety about “what did I do last night” is a question about the gaze of the Other. It helps to distinguish what really happened from what the judge inside fills in.
hangover.practice: Step outside for five minutes and on the way go through two lists in your head: “what I know for sure” and “what the judge fills in.” Notice which is longer.

euphoria.text: An eighteen-month-old recognizes himself in the mirror for the first time — and exults: there he is, whole, put together. Lacan began his theory with this scene, and something of it is in every burst of euphoria, when anything seems possible. In Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego, Freud observed that a feeling of triumph arises when something in us coincides with our “ego ideal” — the image of who we would like to be. For a moment the distance between “who I am” and “who I want to be” vanishes, and everything feels light and bright. Euphoria is not a deception but a precious moment of coinciding with yourself. Psychoanalysis only adds that such coincidence is by nature temporary, because desire lives on distance. That is no reason to cloud the high, but a reason to enjoy it without demanding that it last forever.
euphoria.practice: Look at yourself in the mirror in this moment of elation and name aloud the image you are matching right now: “brave,” “light,” “free.” Remember it — it’s a clue to your ideals, not a promise of forever.

crash.text: “A festival is a permitted, or rather an obligatory, excess,” Freud wrote in Totem and Taboo. And after the festival comes the drop: the world fades, and it seems it will always be like this. Freud described how, after a festival or a moment of triumph, the ego and the ego ideal part ways again: the distance between who we are and who we want to be reappears, and it feels like a loss. Lacan would add that achieved things often lose their shine: the familiar “that’s not it.” The comedown is neither proof that the joy was fake nor the truth about your life. It is the return of lack, from which desire is born. The slump will pass, and lack will once again become what moves you.
crash.practice: Stay silent for a minute after the words “Right now I’m missing…”, without filling the pause — like an analyst who lets an important word resound. Lack is part of being alive.

panic.text: Freud was one of the first to describe the panic attack — back in 1895, long before it had that name. It is genuinely frightening: your heart, your breathing, the feeling “I’m about to die or go mad.” Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. He distinguished two kinds of anxiety. “Signal” anxiety warns of danger. “Automatic” anxiety floods us when the psyche can’t process tension in time — Freud saw its prototype in the helplessness of infancy. Lacan would say that in such moments we collide with the “Real” — what cannot be put into words. So two things help: support for the body now, and words later. Once the wave has passed, telling the story of it already begins to make it less formless.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel them. Make your exhale longer than your inhale and name aloud what you see: “table, window, cup” — word by word, like threads with which the symbolic stitches you back to reality.

dread.text: “No one believes in his own death,” Freud wrote in 1915, in the middle of a war. When “what is all this for” rises up, the sense of the abyss and of finitude, there is nothing abnormal about it. In “Thoughts for the Times on War and Death” he explained that it is impossible truly to imagine our own death: in the unconscious each of us is, as it were, convinced of our own immortality. That is why the thought of finitude intrudes as something alien and frightening. Lacan called the “Real” whatever doesn’t fit into language and images — and dread arises when we come too close to it. The answer is not to find a final explanation but to keep speaking: language, bonds with people, desire — these are what human beings build at the edge of the abyss, and that building is life itself.
dread.practice: Call or send a message to someone you’ve long wanted to talk to — just “how are you?”. Lacan would say that at the edge of the abyss people build speech and bonds; this is one small brick of that building.

fomo.text: “Man’s desire is the desire of the Other” — Lacan’s most quoted formula, and any feed confirms it every second. The feeling that everyone is living more interesting lives while you are “in the wrong place” is common and painful. The formula means that our desire is always bound up with the Other. We want not simply things but what others find desirable, what seems recognized. Social media is the perfect machine for this desire: it shows not people’s lives but their shop window, an “imaginary” image in Lacan’s sense. The fear of missing out is less about events than about the question: “Where is the thing I actually want?” You won’t find the answer in someone else’s feed. Lacan considered the central ethical question to be “Have you acted in conformity with the desire that is in you?” — in you, specifically.
fomo.practice: Ask yourself aloud about whatever triggered the fear of missing out: “Do I want this — or do I want to be seen there?” Say both versions and listen to which one sounds truer.

sleepless.text: At three in the morning the unconscious speaks louder — at last nothing is interrupting it. If you can’t sleep and the thoughts are wearing you out, psychoanalysis has an image for this. Freud called the dream the “guardian of sleep”: it turns anxious thoughts into images so that we can keep sleeping. When there is too much anxiety, this guardian can’t cope, and we wake up or can’t fall asleep. Night thoughts are not the truth about your life but material the psyche didn’t manage to process during the day. Lacan would stress that the unconscious speaks in language: a recurring night thought is like a sentence that hasn’t yet been heard to the end. You don’t need to resolve it at night. It’s enough to write it down and save it for a daytime conversation, with yourself or someone else.
sleepless.practice: Write down the night thought in one sentence, exactly as it sounds, and lay the sheet face down: “until morning.” In the morning, underline the most important word in it.

quote.text: Dreams are the guardians of sleep and not its disturbers.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

betrayal.text: “You are my wife”: Lacan cited these words as an example of “full speech,” which doesn’t describe a bond but creates it. That is why betrayal wounds so deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but your picture of the world. Lacan distinguished two levels of relationship. The “imaginary” is the level of images: we see in the other who we would like them to be. The “symbolic” is the level of the word, of promises, of agreement, on which trust rests. Betrayal breaks one’s word, striking at what life among people depends on. Lacan also said that the Other is always “incomplete”: no person can be a total guarantee. Betrayal doesn’t prove you were foolish. It painfully reveals what no one wants to know: there are no guarantees, and yet people go on giving their word.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence: “I believed that he/she…” — and read it aloud. Listen: is this about the real person, or about an image you loved?

jealousy.text: In 1922 Freud made a surprising claim: someone who isn’t jealous at all is most likely just not noticing their jealousy. Jealousy is agonizing, but there’s nothing shameful in it. He counted its “normal” form among the affects better not denied. He distinguished jealousy based on a real threat from “projected” jealousy, in which we attribute our own unconscious desires to the other. Lacan loved an example from Augustine’s Confessions: an infant, pale with jealousy, watches his brother at the breast. For Lacan this is a scene of the “imaginary”: the other seems to possess what we lack. Jealousy often speaks not only of your partner but also of your own lack — and that can be explored without shame.
jealousy.practice: Picture the rival and silently ask them: “What do you have that I don’t?” The first answer is more about your own lack than about them; stay with it for a minute without shame.

resentment.text: “Remembering, Repeating and Working-Through” — Freud titled a paper with three verbs, and all three bear directly on an old grievance. You carry it around, it flares up again and again, and almost always there is a real injustice behind it. In that paper (1914) he noted that what we cannot remember and fully put into words, we tend to repeat. Lacan would add an uncomfortable but freeing thought: in the way we cling to a grievance there is a hidden jouissance of its own — the bitter satisfaction of being right, a bond with the one who hurt us that won’t let us release them. This doesn’t mean “it’s your own fault”: this is how the psyche works for everyone. A grievance needs not prohibition but working-through — finally being spoken in full.
resentment.practice: Tell your grievance aloud from beginning to end — to one person or to an empty room — as if for the last time. Lacan would say: what has been fully spoken holds on less tightly.

heartbreak.text: Lacan said that in love we give our lack — and a breakup returns it with interest, suddenly and sharply. A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it needs time. Freud described this state with rare precision. In “Mourning and Melancholia,” he speaks of the “work of mourning”: slowly, one memory at a time, the psyche withdraws its attachment from a person who is no longer there. It is agonizing precisely because it happens gradually, and each memory has to be lived through again. Your pain is work that is taking its course. It can’t be hurried by command, but you can avoid getting in its way: let yourself remember, talk, cry.
heartbreak.practice: Walk for ten minutes and on the way go through one memory of the person — slowly, in detail, to the end. Freud would call this a step in the “work of mourning”: memory lets go piece by piece.

quote.text: We are never so defenceless against suffering as when we love, never so helplessly unhappy as when we have lost our loved object or its love.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

impostor.text: “A king who believes he is a king is no less mad than a madman,” Lacan liked to say. If you fear being “found out” any minute, that line is unexpectedly on your side. Freud described the paradox of “those wrecked by success”: sometimes a person struggles not with failure but precisely with the fulfilment of a wish, as if they had no right to it. Lacan went further. In his view, every role we have — “doctor,” “manager,” “specialist” — is given to us from outside, from the symbolic order, rather than growing out of our nature. So everyone who is honest with themselves feels a gap between themselves and their title. Remember his king. Your gap is not exposure but a sign of sobriety.
impostor.practice: Name your role aloud — “doctor,” “manager,” “mom” — and then three things you actually do in it. The role may be borrowed clothes, but the work is yours.

quote.text: If a man who thinks he is a king is mad, a king who thinks he is a king is no less so.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan

self_hatred.text: Freud noticed something strange: the cruelest reproaches a melancholic aims at himself often fit not him but someone else. When an inner voice keeps saying you are worthless, it hurts terribly, but that voice is wrong, even if it sounds convincing. Freud called this agency the “superego” and noticed its strangeness: the stricter a person is with themselves, the harsher it becomes — obedience never satisfies it. In “Mourning and Melancholia,” he suggested that such self-reproaches are really addressed to someone else — an important person one wasn’t allowed to be angry with — and have been turned inward. The inner critic is not the voice of truth about you but someone else’s voice, absorbed long ago. Psychoanalysis doesn’t suggest arguing with it, but asking: whose words are these? Once you recognize them, it’s easier to stop taking them for your own.
self_hatred.practice: Say your inner critic’s most frequent phrase aloud and ask: “Whose voice is this? Who once spoke to me like this?” Repeat it in that intonation: what belongs to someone else is easier to recognize by ear.

helplessness.text: Each of us began unable even to turn over alone, able only to call out. Helplessness is a heavy and ancient feeling, and Freud saw the key to it in this beginning. Freud believed that human life begins with it: for a long time an infant cannot help itself, and this original helplessness (Hilflosigkeit) makes us creatures who need others. That is why, for Freud, in moments of adult powerlessness a very early, almost childlike fear returns so easily. Your feeling is not evidence of weakness but the echo of a deep experience shared by all people. There’s something else too: out of infant helplessness grew not only anxiety but also speech and connection with others. The answer to helplessness has essentially always been to reach out — a request, a story, a call. That is still a possible step now.
helplessness.practice: Call out to someone — by message or by voice — and ask for one small thing: help, a listening ear, simply being nearby. For Freud, calling out is a human being’s very first answer to helplessness.

procrastination.text: Freud wrote a whole book with “inhibition” in its title — and approached it with curiosity, not reproach. If you just can’t get started, it isn’t laziness, and psychoanalysis sees it the same way. Inhibition, for Freud, is when the psyche restricts some activity so as not to run into anxiety. Sometimes starting is frightening because a beginning brings closer an evaluation, a possible failure — or, on the contrary, success and the expectations that come with it. Lacan noted that desire is often sustained by what remains unfulfilled: as long as the task hasn’t been started, it can be as perfect as you like. Procrastination is a message, not a defect: something about the task is making you anxious. What helps is not pressure but a question: what will change if I begin?
procrastination.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I start this, I’ll have to face…” — and look at the last word. Then take the smallest possible first step: just open the file.

uprooted.text: In 1938 Freud, eighty-two and gravely ill, left Vienna for London and took his couch with him. Being cut off from home — losing your ground, your language, familiar faces, the life you were used to — is a real loss, and it deserves to be mourned. He knew that loss from the inside. Lacan emphasized that the human being exists in language: our “native” language is not a tool but the fabric our “I” is made of. That’s why living in a foreign language can sometimes feel like living slightly outside your own skin. In his essay “The Uncanny,” Freud noted that the German word unheimlich (uncanny) comes from Heim — home. Your longing is grief that needs time and words, in any language.
uprooted.practice: Say aloud a phrase in your native language that you haven’t spoken in a long time — a saying, a line, a word used only at home. Listen to how your voice sounds in it: Lacan would say this is the fabric your “I” is made of.

overload.text: Freud has an image of a tiny living vesicle that survives only because its outer layer hardens into a shield against stimuli. The feed, the notifications and the endless stream wear you out, and it seems there’s no free space left inside. The psyche, for Freud, is shielded the same way from too strong a flow of impressions, and when this shield is breached, an overload arises that it can’t keep up with. Lacan would add something unexpected: our superego can not only forbid but also command “Enjoy!” — watch more, learn more, don’t miss out. Endless scrolling is not weakness of will but a response to that command. You can allow yourself what this voice can’t stand: to stop, to not know everything, to leave something unread.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down and for ten minutes find out nothing: no reading, no scrolling, no checking. Tell yourself: “No ‘enjoy!’ today” — and notice what happens in your body.

unreality.text: In 1904 Freud climbed the Acropolis and suddenly thought: “So all this really does exist?” If everything around you, or you yourself, doesn’t feel quite real right now, it’s strange and frightening, and it deserves gentle care. More than thirty years later, in “A Disturbance of Memory on the Acropolis” (1936), he described the strange estrangement he had felt: as if what he was seeing wasn’t entirely real. Freud didn’t decide he was “broken”; he set out to explore what the feeling meant, and linked it to deep experiences from his past. For psychoanalysis, a feeling of unreality is also a message: sometimes this is how the psyche holds at a distance what is too much to feel directly right now. You don’t have to fight it; you can calmly lean on sensations and words.
unreality.practice: Describe aloud what you see, as if telling a friend on the phone: “In front of me there’s a table, a cup on it, and outside the window…” Words are what the symbolic uses to stitch you back to the world.

quote.text: So all this really does exist, just as we learnt at school!
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: A Disturbance of Memory on the Acropolis (1936)

awe.text: Romain Rolland wrote to Freud about a feeling he called “oceanic” — a sense of connection with something limitless. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare experience of the same kind. Freud admitted that he himself hardly knew it, but he took it seriously and suggested that it recalls a very early state, when the “I” had not yet separated from the world. Lacan described “sublimation” as raising an object “to the dignity of the Thing” — when something ordinary suddenly glows with something greater than itself. Awe is a moment when the boundary between you and the world grows thin for a second. It doesn’t need to be fully explained; you can simply treasure it.
awe.practice: Go out under the sky or to a window and for a minute look at the biggest thing you can see, without naming it. Then try in one sentence — and notice what words can’t convey: that is Lacan’s Real.

relief.text: One of psychoanalysis’s first patients, Anna O., called the talking treatment “chimney sweeping.” Relief is familiar to anyone who has talked something out: something lets go, you can breathe out, and it’s worth accepting without reservations. Freud believed that the psyche is largely governed by the “pleasure principle” — the drive to reduce painful tension. Relief is the experience of that reduction in its pure form. Back in Studies on Hysteria, Freud and Breuer noticed that when a painful experience can be put into words, liberation follows — they called this “catharsis.” And in his book on jokes, Freud wrote that laughter arises when energy we had been spending on holding back is released. Relief shows how much strength was going into the tension. You can take note of exactly what eased it.
relief.practice: Tell someone in two sentences what exactly eased the tension — “sweep the chimney,” as Anna O. put it. Relief spoken aloud is remembered better.

calm.text: Freud asked analysts to listen in a special way: grasping at nothing and pushing nothing away. Calm, which needs no justification, is a little like that kind of listening. Oddly enough, psychoanalysis knows a lot about calm, because it knows a lot about unrest. For Lacan, the human being is a desiring creature, and desire never falls completely silent. So calm is not the absence of desire but a moment when it doesn’t press or demand to get something urgently. Freud called this listening “evenly suspended attention.” Your calm is like that kind of attention to your own life: anything can be, and nothing is needed right now. You can simply be in this state.
calm.practice: For a minute, listen to the sounds around you with “evenly suspended attention”: singling none out and pushing none away. Like an analyst who is silent and simply hears.

inspiration.text: “Before the problem of the creative artist analysis must, alas, lay down its arms,” Freud admitted. Inspiration, the vivid state in which you want to create, stays a bit of a mystery — but psychoanalysis does know something about it. Freud used the word “sublimation” for the process by which powerful drives find a new path — into art, science, work — and saw it as one of civilization’s highest achievements. Lacan rethought sublimation as the capacity to raise an ordinary object “to the dignity of the Thing”: a word, a sound, a line suddenly begins to carry something greater than itself. It is the moment when your desire finds a form. Lacan believed it matters not to give ground on your desire. So it’s good to give inspiration an outlet straight away, while the desire is hot — without judging, comparing, or asking whether anyone needs it.
inspiration.practice: Give your inspiration a form within ten minutes: a sketch, a note, a couple of lines, a tune on a voice recorder. Don’t edit — Lacan would say the main thing now is not to give ground on your desire.

schadenfreude.text: In his book on jokes, Freud noticed that many jokes are permitted aggression — a blow you are allowed to land with a smile. Schadenfreude, pleasure at someone else’s failure, is usually embarrassing to admit even to yourself. But psychoanalysis begins precisely by not turning away from such feelings. Lacan described the “mirror stage”: our ego is formed from an image, and next to it there is always a double — another who resembles us, with whom we compete for place and recognition. He called this dimension the “imaginary.” When a rival stumbles, for a moment it seems there is more room for us. Schadenfreude is not proof of your malice but a trace of this old struggle for a place. You can notice it and ask: who am I comparing myself with right now?
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine that the rival who stumbled is your reflection in a mirror. Ask: “If they lost, then I…?” — and finish it aloud. The answer will show what rivalry lives in you.

contempt.text: “The narcissism of minor differences” — that is how Freud explained why we push away most strongly those who resemble us. Contempt seems cold and confident, but something vulnerable often hides behind it. In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) he gave examples: neighbors, relatives, closely related groups. A small difference is needed to emphasize one’s own separateness. And in “On the Universal Tendency to Debasement in the Sphere of Love” (1912), he showed how the psyche can divide people into the exalted and the “low” in order to cope with an inner conflict. Contempt often pushes away in another what too closely resembles ourselves, or what we don’t want to see in ourselves. This doesn’t make you a bad person. It makes contempt interesting: you can question it.
contempt.practice: Name aloud the trait you despise in this person, then quietly ask: “Has it ever — even a little — been in me?” A minor difference sometimes turns out to be very minor indeed.

disgust.text: In 1905 Freud called disgust, shame and morality “dams” — mental forces that grow up to restrain and channel the drives. Disgust is a strong bodily feeling, whether directed at others, at a situation or at yourself, and it doesn’t make you bad. He also noted that intense disgust is sometimes a “reaction formation”: the psyche turns attraction into repulsion so as not to encounter a desire. This doesn’t mean that a desire hides behind every disgust — often it simply protects. But disgust is worth not only enduring but also listening to: it speaks of a boundary that matters to you, and sometimes of something that has come too close to that boundary.
disgust.practice: Imagine your disgust as a dam and ask it aloud: “What are you protecting me from right now?” Don’t judge the first answer — just hear it.

revenge.text: “Where id was, there ego shall be” — that is how Freud put the aim of analysis. The wish for revenge usually grows out of a real hurt: you were caused pain, and justice demands a response. Freud did not consider people naturally peaceful: in Civilization and Its Discontents he wrote about a deep-rooted inclination to aggression that civilization is forced to restrain somehow. But psychoanalysis draws a strict line between thought and deed. Fantasies of revenge can be stormy — they are psychic reality, not a crime. The danger lies in “acting them out,” bypassing words. That is his formula: where an impersonal drive operates, an “I” should appear that can become aware of it and choose. Revenge can be given a place in words — in writing, in conversation — and then it stops giving the orders.
revenge.practice: Write a letter to the person who hurt you that you will never send — with all your anger, uncensored — and tear it up. Then say aloud what you wanted most: punishment, acknowledgment, or an apology.

quote.text: Where id was, there ego shall be.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.source: New Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis (1933), Lecture 31

anger_at_loved.text: An infant sees its mother now as “good,” now as “bad,” and only gradually understands that she is one person. Anger at a partner, parents, children can burn, and shame follows — but here psychoanalysis is rather reassuring. Melanie Klein showed that the mixing of love and anger begins right there. Klein called this step the “depressive position” — not an illness but a stage of growing up, in which we learn to bear that the one we love and the one we are angry with are the same person. From this comes the wish for “reparation” — to make amends, to take care, to restore the bond. Anger does not cancel love. What matters is neither to pour it out on the person you love nor to hide it from yourself, but to give it words — and then to come back with care.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger has calmed, say one warm sentence to the person — not an apology for the feeling, but a sign of connection: “I was angry, and you matter to me.” Klein would call it a small reparation.

ambivalence.text: Lacan coined a word, hainamoration — “hateloving” — fusing hatred and being in love into one. To love and be unable to stand the same person at the same time is agonizing, but it is one of the most common human experiences. The word “ambivalence” itself was introduced by the psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler, and Freud made it one of his key concepts: in Totem and Taboo (1913) he showed that toward the most important people — parents, lovers, teachers — our feelings are almost inevitably double. Mixed feelings don’t mean that something in the relationship is irreparably broken or that you “don’t know how to love.” Rather, they mean this person truly matters to you. You don’t have to resolve the ambivalence immediately; you can let both sides speak.
ambivalence.practice: Read the word “hateloving” aloud and listen: there’s no “but” in it; both feelings hold together. Try, in the same single breath, to say about this person both what you love and what you can’t stand.

guilty_relief.text: In Totem and Taboo Freud noted that after a loved one’s death people often torment themselves with reproaches, as if they were guilty of something. A similar shame often comes with relief after a breakup, a death, or a long illness: how can I feel lighter? But relief and love can live side by side. Freud explained such reproaches by saying that in any deep attachment, besides tenderness, there is also weariness and hidden resentment, which we are ashamed of and don’t acknowledge. Relief is partly the voice of that unacknowledged weariness. And it doesn’t cancel love or mean you are a bad person. It may mean that a long strain has ended — and it can give you the strength to grieve for real.
guilty_relief.practice: Write two sentences side by side: “I feel lighter because what has ended is…” and “I miss…”. Read them aloud one after the other — both are true.

indifference.text: Sometimes feeling arrives not when it “should” but a week later — over a sad film or spilled coffee. Where something “ought” to move you — someone else’s misfortune, important news, even a loss — there may be silence inside. It’s frightening, but indifference rarely means you truly don’t care. Freud described a mechanism he called “isolation”: the psyche separates an idea from the affect attached to it, so that an event can be known without being felt at full strength. He also noted that affect can “relocate,” appearing later over some trivial occasion. Numbness is not coldness but a form of defense, often temporary: the psyche is protecting you until it is ready to take in what happened. There’s no need to force yourself to feel “the right way.” You can simply note: my feelings are on pause — and let them come in their own time.
indifference.practice: Sit in silence for a minute, demanding no feelings of yourself, like an analyst who knows how to wait. Say to yourself: “Feelings on pause are an answer too.”

escape.text: Freud compared fantasy to a nature reserve: a patch of wild land kept as it was while civilization changed everything around it. The wish to drop everything and leave — your job, your city, your familiar role — is such a reserve: often it is the voice of weariness with a life that has become too cramped. Lacan described desire as “metonymy”: it slides from object to object, aimed not at a thing but at a lack no thing fully closes. Freud showed that fantasies are not empty daydreams but scenes in which we fulfil our wishes. It is worth listening seriously to your escape fantasy: who do you become there, whose gaze are you freed from, what do you finally allow yourself? Often “drop everything” means “stop living up to other people’s expectations.” You can understand this without making any big decisions yet.
escape.practice: Close your eyes and for two minutes stay inside your escape fantasy, as in a nature reserve: where you are, what you’re doing, who isn’t around. When you open your eyes, name the one thing you want most there — no decisions.

forbidden_attraction.text: “I would not have known sin except through the law” — Lacan read these words of the apostle Paul in his seminar on ethics as a description of desire itself. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” can be confusing and frightening. But in itself it says nothing about what you will do, and psychoanalysis approaches it without moralizing. Lacan concluded that prohibition and desire are more tightly linked than they seem: what is “forbidden” itself becomes attractive. Moreover, for Lacan, desire is aimed not so much at a person as at the “object a” — the elusive cause of desire, which always slips away a little. It’s useful to ask not “Is this right?” but “What in me responds to this unavailability?”
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine that the prohibition suddenly vanished: this person is free and available. What happens to the attraction — does it grow or fade? Just observe, with no conclusions or decisions.

social_anxiety.text: Lacan spoke of the “big Other” — an authority before which we seem to be forever sitting an exam. When fear of judgment makes simple things hard — walking into a room, starting a conversation, making a call — that examiner is especially loud. Lacan described how, at the “mirror stage,” a child recognizes itself in its reflection and turns to an adult for confirmation: “Is that me?” From then on, part of our ego rests on another’s gaze and approval. This big Other is language, rules, an imaginary judge. But the real people in the room are usually far less preoccupied with us than the inner examiner is. You can gradually learn to tell living companions apart from the onlooker we carry inside.
social_anxiety.practice: At a gathering, pick one real person and for a minute simply watch what they’re busy with: where they look, what they hold. Most likely they’re occupied with themselves, not you — the examiner lives only inside.

uncertainty.text: “The subject supposed to know” — that is what Lacan called the analyst, and a whole philosophy hides in that “supposed.” Uncertainty is exhausting: you can’t plan, there’s nothing to lean on, and you wish someone knew the answer. Here psychoanalysis says something unexpected: no one has complete knowledge. A person comes to an analyst hoping that someone knows the answer, and gradually discovers that no such all-knowing Other exists. Lacan depicted this as the “barred” Other: language, society, authorities are incomplete too. At first this is frightening, but there is freedom in it as well: if no one knows for sure, then your not knowing is not a personal failure but a shared condition of life. Even Freud, in his late paper “Analysis Terminable and Interminable” (1937), admitted that the work of understanding itself is never finished. Uncertainty can be carried as a shared burden.
uncertainty.practice: Write down the question that torments you, and beneath it: “Right now nobody knows this — not even the big Other.” Read it aloud and notice how the feeling changes.

waiting.text: The most famous game in the history of psychoanalysis is a game about waiting. When you’re waiting for an answer, results, news, time stretches and everything seems on pause. Freud once watched his eighteen-month-old grandson playing with a wooden reel on a string: he would throw it over the edge of his cot with a long “o-o-o-o” (Freud understood it as fort — “gone”) and joyfully pull it back: da — “there.” He described this game in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) and interpreted it this way: the child, waiting for his absent mother, was turning helpless waiting into an action of his own, one he could control. Waiting is especially agonizing when we are completely passive. Finding in it even a small area where you act for yourself makes it more bearable.
waiting.practice: Play “fort — da”: toss something soft away and bring it back, saying “gone — there.” Then do one small task that depends only on you while there’s still no answer.

regret.text: The past can’t be remade, but it can be retold — in essence, the whole of psychoanalysis rests on this. Regret that returns again and again says that something mattered to you. Psychoanalysis offers two ways of looking at it. Freud wrote about “deferred action” (Nachträglichkeit): the meaning of past events can change later, when we learn and live through something new. Retelling changes what the past means for you. And in The Ethics of Psychoanalysis, Lacan gave a provocative formula: true guilt lies in giving ground on your own desire, in betraying it. Regret sometimes points not to a mistake to be mourned endlessly, but to a desire that is still alive and can be heard now.
regret.practice: Retell the story you regret to someone — or aloud to yourself — but begin with the words “What I really wanted back then was…”. Notice whether the meaning shifts in the retelling.

quote.text: The only thing one can be guilty of is having given ground relative to one’s desire.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar VII: The Ethics of Psychoanalysis (1959–1960)

longing.text: What do we lose when someone we love is no longer near? Lacan would answer: more than that one person. Missing them can be almost physical: you miss their voice, their look, their presence. In “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), Freud described the “work of mourning”: slowly, memory by memory, the soul relives each thread connecting it to the one who is absent, and only in this way gradually frees its energy for life. It can’t be hurried by command. Lacan would add that the person we love was for us not only themselves but also a place where we felt desired and seen. So we long both for them and for the self we were beside them. Longing is work that a loving soul does. It can be lived through gently, a little at a time.
longing.practice: Say aloud one pet word or phrase this person used to say — in their intonation. Listen to how it sounds in your voice: this is how the bond goes on living in speech.

world_pain.text: “Why war?” Einstein asked Freud in 1932, and Freud replied with a long letter. Pain for the world — injustice, grim news — can press so hard that ordinary life gets difficult, and it speaks of your capacity for compassion. In 1915, at the height of the First World War, Freud wrote “Thoughts for the Times on War and Death,” in which he confessed to the same disillusionment and bewilderment that many felt. And he ended his reply to Einstein on a note of cautious hope: whatever fosters the growth of civilization and the ties between people works against destruction. Your pain is not naivety but part of those ties. But the psyche can’t hold other people’s suffering without limit. Taking care of your strength is not indifference but the condition for going on feeling.
world_pain.practice: Support one concrete bond today — call, help, take part. Then choose a time of day without news and spend it with what is near: people, a book, a walk.

rejection.text: “Narcissistic wound” — Freud’s term for wounds that strike not the body but the self-image. Rejection hurts as though it weren’t a request that was refused, but you as a whole. Freud wrote about “narcissism” not in the everyday sense of vanity but as the healthy self-love everyone needs. Rejection inflicts a “narcissistic wound”: it strikes at the self-image we build partly out of how others receive us. Lacan showed that our ego is formed from the very beginning out of reflections — out of what we see in the mirror and in other people’s eyes. So someone else’s “no” can feel like a crack in the ego itself. It’s important to remember: a reflection is not yet you. One person’s refusal speaks of a meeting of two desires that didn’t match, not of your worth.
rejection.practice: Ask yourself two questions aloud: “What exactly in me, as it seems, was rejected?” and “Is this a fact, or a reflection I’ve mistaken for myself?” The answers don’t have to be final.

abandonment.text: A child cries when its mother leaves the room — and one day stops, because it carries her image inside. The fear of being abandoned can be very deep and very old: it seems that without the other the ground will give way. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety (1926), Freud considered the loss of a loved person, and later the loss of their love, to be among a child’s earliest situations of danger. Melanie Klein described how a child gradually “takes in” a good image of the caring adult, and this inner support remains even when the real person leaves the room. Your present fear may carry an echo of very old experience. And at the same time, you most likely already have inner supports — people, voices, memories that have stayed with you.
abandonment.practice: Recall someone with whom you felt safe, and say aloud, in their place, one sentence they might say to you now. That is the inner support Klein wrote about.

unrequited.text: “I love in you something more than you” — that is how Lacan described love, which always slightly misses the living person. When the feeling is there but no answer comes, it hurts, but the love is no less real for that. In “On Narcissism” (1914), Freud noted that being in love is often accompanied by “overvaluation” of the beloved: they are endowed with perfections that largely belong to our own ideal. Lacan went further: that something more is the mysterious “object a,” which causes desire but never coincides with the living person. That is why unrequited love wounds twice over: we lose not only hope in the person but also the ideal we invested in them. You can try to discern what exactly you loved in them — and which part of it is really yours and can stay with you.
unrequited.practice: Write down three qualities you love in this person, and circle the ones you’d like to find or develop in your own life. That is the part of love that stays yours.

humiliation.text: Someone rises by lowering another — that, for Lacan, is how the play of images works, the register he called the “imaginary.” When you’ve been humiliated, often in front of others, it feels as though your dignity has been taken. Freud distinguished the ego from the “ego ideal” — the image of who we would like to be. Humiliation strikes precisely at the gap between them: we are, as it were, forcibly shown to be far from our own ideal. Lacan would add that humiliation unfolds precisely in this register. But the image imposed on you is not the whole truth about you: the subject, for Lacan, is always more than any reflection. You can separate the pain, which is real, from the verdict, which you don’t have to accept.
humiliation.practice: Stand up straight and feel your feet and the crown of your head — a body greater than any reflection. Say aloud: “This image was imposed on me. I am more than it.”

body_shame.text: “The ego is first and foremost a bodily ego,” Freud wrote. When the mirror becomes an exam and dissatisfaction with your body wears you out, that line is easy to forget. In his paper on the “mirror stage” (1949), Lacan described how an infant, still clumsy and uncoordinated, suddenly sees a unified image in the mirror — and joyfully takes it for itself. Ever since, according to Lacan, a tension lives in us between how the body feels from the inside and a picture that “ought” to be smooth and whole. Body shame is not your personal whim but a crack built into the very way we become ourselves. It can be softened by returning more often from the picture to the living sensation: the body is not only an image but also the one who feels.
body_shame.practice: Turn away from the mirror and for a minute feel your body from the inside: the warmth of your hands, your weight, your breathing. This is the “bodily ego” the reflection doesn’t show.

quote.text: The ego is first and foremost a bodily ego; it is not merely a surface entity, but is itself the projection of a surface.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud

illness.text: The poet Wilhelm Busch has a line Freud quoted: a man with toothache has his whole soul living “in his molar’s narrow hole.” When your body lets you down — pain, illness, weakness — it’s hard, and irritation, fear and sadness are natural here. In “On Narcissism” (1914), Freud observed that a person tormented by pain or illness involuntarily withdraws interest from the outside world and concentrates on themselves. Freud didn’t condemn this — he saw in it a natural movement of the psyche gathering its forces where it hurts. If right now it’s hard to be interested in anything but your own condition, that isn’t selfishness. Interest in the world usually returns when things get a little easier; for now, you can simply be more attentive to yourself.
illness.practice: Say aloud to yourself one sentence you would say to a sick friend — gentle, without demands: “This is hard for you right now; you don’t have to decide anything.” Repeat it when things get heavier.

pride.text: Whose face did you picture when it all worked out? Lacan would find that question important. Pride in what you’ve done is deserved, and there’s no need to hide it. For Freud, everyone needs healthy self-love, and an important part of it is the sense of having come closer to your “ego ideal,” the image of who you want to be. When that happens, self-regard rises, and that is good. Freud called channeling the drives into work, creativity and knowledge “sublimation,” and pride often accompanies such fruits. Lacan would add: it matters whose recognition you are seeking. Pride is steadiest when you yourself see the value of your work, not only others’ applause. You can allow yourself to rejoice — and notice which of your own desires has come true.
pride.practice: Tell one person what you’ve done, and add: “This matters to me because…”. Lacan would ask whose recognition you’re seeking; let the first be your own.

melancholy.text: In the summer of 1913 Freud went walking in the mountains with a young poet who could not enjoy beauty knowing it would fade. Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow mixes with tenderness toward the world, and Freud’s argument with the poet is precisely about it. It’s important to make a distinction right away: for Freud, “melancholia” is a clinical concept describing a severe condition, while gentle sadness is something quite different. Closer to it is Freud’s short essay “On Transience” (1916). Freud objected: transience does not take value away from beauty; on the contrary, it adds to it. Gentle sadness is a way of feeling the value of what passes. You can live through it unhurriedly, like quiet music, without turning it into anxiety about loss.
melancholy.practice: Read aloud Freud’s line from “On Transience”: “Transience value is scarcity value in time.” Then spend a minute with something passing nearby — a light, a smell, a sound.

quote.text: Transience value is scarcity value in time.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
